bottomLine: You already carry €9.3M in traced EU and Dutch public capital since 2022, close to LioniX International's €13.0M and ahead of New Origin's €997K, so evaluators in this cluster already know how to fund a Dutch photonics foundry.
The NL-EZK-B&I-I&K-RVO NXTGEN HIGHTECH scheme is your strongest first move. It is a national grant under GBER Art. 25 and peers VLC Photonics and LioniX drew €5.4M and €5.2M through it.
EIC Accelerator suits your scaling stage: it pays a grant up to €2.5M and can add €0.5M to €10M in equity from the EIC Fund, matching the ticket size you are seeking.
Chase the NXTGEN HIGHTECH grant alongside a co-financed regional line such as OPZuid in Noord-Brabant, since your own project funding covers over half the cost these schemes leave with you.
Together these routes offer a non-dilutive grant path into the tens of millions, with equity only entering if you choose the EIC's blended option.

report.positioning: The Chips Joint Undertaking and the European Commission are advancing a Chips Act 2.0, and a Semiconductor Alliance of industrial actors including ASML has been consulting on the next phase of Europe's chip strategy. As an indium phosphide photonic integrated circuits foundry, your work sits inside exactly the semiconductor value chain this policy push is meant to strengthen. Frame applications, particularly EIC Accelerator and the Chips JU-adjacent national schemes, around foundry capacity and manufacturing sovereignty in photonic integration rather than around research novelty alone: that is the argument the current chips agenda is built to reward. Your existing Chips JU award of €2.8M already places you inside this strategic-autonomy narrative, which strengthens the case for framing new applications as continuity of that same public-private chips effort rather than a fresh pitch.
report.stateOfPlay: The EIC Accelerator has opened a new €100M defence-focused call and a humanitarian innovation prize, both signalling that the EIC is broadening its tracks rather than only expanding the standard Accelerator route you would apply through. Chips JU is introducing a formal impact monitoring framework for its funded projects, which could add reporting obligations to future calls in the semiconductor line you already draw funding from. Separately, Chips Act 2.0 is moving through consultation with the Semiconductor Alliance, and any resulting change to the Chips JU's scope or state-aid treatment would bear directly on your existing Chips JU relationship and on how national schemes like NXTGEN HIGHTECH are framed for chip manufacturers going forward.
report.caveats: Figures shown are committed amounts from public registers on each instrument's own reporting basis, coverage varies by country, and absence from the database is not proof that no funding was received.

bottomLine: Neura Robotics has €4.3M in traced public funding, a 2022-2025 state aid award, while sector peers Wandercraft and PAL Robotics drew €25.4M and €9.5M respectively through EIB debt and Horizon grants.

At 250+ staff you exceed the EU SME ceiling, so EIC Accelerator and SME-only lanes are closed to you as a solo applicant; EIC Transition stays open but only if you enter as part of a 2-5 entity consortium.

The Horizon Europe clusters (CL1, CL3, CL4, Mission) and Innovation Fund are your real doors given your scale: multi-partner grants and large capex support built for companies at your size and ticket range.
Innovation Fund Smart Systems and Products fits your capex profile directly: grants from €2.5M up to tens of millions for industrial-scale deployment, with no equity attached.
A Horizon Europe consortium slot commonly returns €0.5M-€5M per partner in non-dilutive grant funding, stacked across a multi-year project.

report.positioning: Frame Neura Robotics against the Commission's push to consolidate research and industrial funding into fewer, larger instruments. DG GROW's proposed European Competitiveness Fund, worth €234 billion from 2028, folds Horizon Europe into four windows, with Digital leadership at €51.5 billion and Resilience, security, defence, industry and space at €125.2 billion. Your cognitive humanoid and cobot systems for industrial automation sit squarely inside the digital and industrial-resilience priorities these windows are built around. Because the window allocations and eligibility rules are still being negotiated with the Council and Parliament, position your Horizon Europe applications now around industrial automation and digital leadership framing, since that alignment is what the successor fund is expected to carry forward. Your scale, 250+ staff and a project ticket of €15M-€50M, also matches the profile the Innovation Fund's large-scale industrial window is built for, so frame your capex ask in terms of industrial deployment at scale rather than early-stage R&D, which is the register the GBER rules and the Innovation Fund's own scoring both reward for a company past the SME threshold.
report.stateOfPlay: The Horizon Europe clusters in your table, CL1 and CL4, sit inside a live restructuring: the Commission proposed on 16 July 2025 to fold Horizon Europe's €175 billion into a new €234 billion European Competitiveness Fund from 2028, consolidating today's clusters into four policy windows. For CL4 specifically, your digital and industrial automation work would land inside the proposed €51.5 billion Digital leadership window or the €125.2 billion Resilience, security, defence, industry and space window, both far larger than CL4's current scope. This means a CL1 or CL4 proposal built today may need to be re-argued against new window criteria once the ECF design is finalised, since eligibility rules and allocations are still being negotiated with the Council and Parliament. The proposed ECF also carries a horizontal InvestEU instrument modelled on a scheme that mobilised nearly €300 billion over four years, which could reshape how blended grant-and-guarantee packages are structured for large-ticket applicants like you once it launches.
report.caveats: Figures shown are committed amounts from public registers as reported on each instrument's own basis, coverage varies by country, and absence from the database is not proof that no funding was received.
